In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

we are now beginning to understand the nature of the most massive star-forming galaxies at high-redshift, and that we have a much better understanding of the star formation history of the universe than we had a few years ago.
submillimeter galaxies, while not being the only contributors, are major contributors to the star formation history at high redshift.
submillimeter galaxies are not the dominant mode of star formation in the universe at any epoch, but they contribute a significant fraction of the star formation at high redshift.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the most luminous dusty starbursts are rare at all times but contribute significantly to the total SFR at all epochs, and that their contribution is not well represented by current ultraviolet-based star formation histories.

the most luminous submillimeter galaxies are massive starbursting galaxies that contribute significantly to the cosmic SFR density at high redshift, but they are not the only star-forming systems at those epochs.

submillimeter galaxy surveys have provided us with the best census of star formation activity in the universe, but the most luminous submillimeter galaxies may be rare and extreme, and their contribution to the star formation rate density may be overestimated.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have identified a complete sample of submillimeter-selected starbursts with spectroscopic redshift measurements, and that these galaxies dominate the SFR density at z > 3.5.
the most luminous star-forming galaxies at z > 5 are not the same objects as at lower redshifts.
